title: What Happens When Blind Timers Wire Superstition Fast?
description:
Behavioral & Circuit Analysis — B. F. Skinner (1948): Operant Conditioning Chamber & Accidental 'Superstition' in the Pigeon, grounded in B. F. Skinner (1948) (Journal of Experimental Psychology). Empirical findings show that in 1948, B. F. Skinner placed eight hungry pigeons maintained at 75 percent of their free-feeding body weight into individual operant conditioning chambers.

At the circuit level, this episode examines how basal ganglia, ventral tegmental area coordinate behavioral and neural responses, alongside evidence that instead of requiring a key peck, a mechanical solenoid swung the grain hopper into reach for 5 seconds at fixed 15-second intervals regardless of what the bird was doing.

Primary Peer-Reviewed Sources:
- B. F. Skinner (1948). 'Superstition' in the pigeon. Journal of Experimental Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0055873
- J. E. Staddon, Virginia L. Simmelhag (1971). The "supersitition" experiment: A reexamination of its implications for the principles of adaptive behavior. Psychological Review. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0030305
- J. E. R. Staddon, D. T. Cerutti (2003). Operant Conditioning. Annual Review of Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev.psych.54.101601.145124

AI Disclosure: Visual reenactments, 3D anatomical models, and narration in this documentary Short were produced with AI synthesis tools from verified peer-reviewed sources.
